customer_question: Including our module's Component QDID together with the newer Host/LL QDID produces a bunch of inter-layer inconsistencies around AoA/AoD and Isochronous features. How do we resolve this without triggering a massive new test requirement?
question_variants: Why does combining these two QDIDs cause so many LL-RFPHY inconsistencies?
Do we have to edit the LL ICS ourselves to fix this?
Can the chip vendor provide a Subset that resolves the conflict for free?
actual_issue: Including the module's Component-level QDID (Core Spec v5.1) together with a newer Core-Spec Host/LL QDID (v5.4) for the product registration produced 13 inter-layer inconsistencies between the LL and RFPHY layers, tied to AoA/AoD and Isochronous features that the newer Host/LL QDID supports but the older Component QDID's RF PHY content does not address, and a way to resolve this without triggering a large new test requirement was needed.
plain_english_explanation: When you combine an older chip-level certification with a newer software-stack certification, the newer one can claim support for advanced features (like direction-finding or isochronous audio channels) that the older certification's radio-testing checklist simply doesn't have entries for, causing a long list of automatic conflicts. Fixing this by directly editing the older certification's checklist would force a huge amount of additional radio testing. The better fix is to ask the company that owns the older certification to issue a trimmed-down version of it with those specific advanced features turned off, which is free and avoids the conflict entirely.
consultant_answer: Including QDID [Component, Core Spec v5.1] together with QDID [Wireless Gecko Link Layer and Host, Core Spec v5.4] produces 13 inter-layer inconsistencies between LL and RFPHY (tied to AoA/AoD and Isochronous functionality), each following the pattern 'If [RFPHY] is Supported and [RFPHY] (item) is Not Supported then [LL] (item) is Excluded.' Modifying the LL ICS directly to resolve this would trigger LL-layer testing requirements numbering in the hundreds of items. Instead, the recommended fix is for the Component QDID's Listing Owner (the chip vendor) to create a free Subset that flips the specific 15 conflicting LL ICS items from Support YES to NO, removing AoA/AoD and Isochronous support from that Subset. If the vendor already has a Subset DN with these features set to NO (from this QDID or an equivalent design registration), that DN can be used directly. The customer confirmed with Silicon Laboratories and received the resolving registration data: a specific QDID for the Component part, together with a specific DN covering the LL, HCI, and Host layers, which eliminated the inconsistency.
decision_logic: When Including a Component-level Controller QDID together with a newer Core-Spec Host/LL QDID produces inter-layer inconsistencies tied to features the newer QDID supports but the Component QDID's RF PHY content does not address (such as AoA/AoD or Isochronous), the correct fix is to request a free Subset from the Component QDID's Listing Owner with the specific conflicting ICS items flipped to NO, rather than editing the LL ICS directly, which would trigger a large new LL-layer test requirement.
final_recommendation: When combining a Component-level Controller QDID with a newer Core-Spec Host/LL QDID produces inter-layer inconsistencies tied to advanced features like AoA/AoD or Isochronous, ask the Component QDID's Listing Owner to create (or provide an existing) free Subset with those specific ICS items set to NO, rather than directly editing the LL ICS and triggering a large new test requirement.
risk_if_done_wrong: Directly editing the LL ICS to resolve the inconsistency, instead of requesting a vendor-issued Subset, would trigger a large new LL-layer test requirement (hundreds of items), adding substantial unplanned cost and schedule to the registration.
